items.concept: agents.md and the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP)
items.summary: agents.md and the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) are the two-layer agent-facing commerce discovery stack Shopify exposes on every storefront: agents.md is the canonical, merchant-authored Markdown signpost (distinct from the unrelated repo-root AGENTS.md coding-agent convention) that points at UCP, the Apache-2.0 machine-readable protocol Google launched with Shopify on 2026-01-11 for capability negotiation, RFC 9421-signed requests, and commerce transactions via /.well-known/ucp and its REST/MCP/A2A/Embedded transports. Summarized from 2 sources (the agents-md.md and ucp-protocol.md hub reference files, each a /dr research pass with live-fetch verification), covering definition, structure, mechanism, examples, measures, problems and facts facets across both the file-collision/rollout side and the protocol/governance/negotiation/signing side.

items.concept: Atlas AI Services Pricing (Agent Engine and Voyage AI)
items.summary: Atlas AI spend has two metered parts: Voyage AI embedding and reranking (per token, or per pixel for multimodal models, with 200 million free tokens for most current models) billed to the Atlas organization that owns the API key, and Automated Embedding in Atlas Vector Search, which uses the same per-token rates and meters initial sync, inserts, updates and queries. Atlas Agent Engine (Agent Runtime and Agent Memory), announced 2026-09-29 in public preview, is consumption-priced and draws down existing Atlas commitments, but no unit rates are published. The pack draws on 6 sources (the Atlas Embedding and Reranking API and Automated Embedding billing pages, the Automated Embedding models page, the Voyage pricing page, a MongoDB press release and IT Brief coverage) and flags 2 disagreements about which reranker and which legacy embedding models receive free tokens.

items.concept: Atlas Billing and Invoice Anatomy
items.summary: Atlas bills at the organization level and posts usage charges the day after they are incurred, itemized on a pending (current) invoice and past invoices. Each invoice page has Payment Details, Total Usage and By Deployment charts, Summary by Project and Summary by Service tables, and a Usage Details line-item layer (dates, quantity in server hours, project, cloud provider, SKU rate, amount). This pack draws on 6 source pages across 2 hosts (MongoDB Atlas billing docs, the Admin API invoice reference, a community forum thread and a OneUptime blog) and covers definitions, structure, mechanism, parameters, how-to, examples, measures and problems.

items.concept: Atlas Cost Explorer and Billing Data API
items.summary: Atlas Cost Explorer is a visual interface in the Billing section of the Atlas UI for viewing and analyzing monthly Atlas usage, visible to the Organization Owner, Billing Admin and Organization Billing Viewer roles. The same billing data is exposed programmatically through the Atlas Administration API as an asynchronous Cost Explorer query (create a query, then poll with a token) and, in the FOCUS 1.3 format, through the FOCUS Data API (list invoices, request a report, retrieve a report); third-party FinOps tools such as OpenCost and DoiT Cloud Intelligence consume it with read-only billing credentials. This pack draws on 8 source pages across 4 host labels and covers definitions, structure, mechanism, parameters (including the FOCUS column reference), how-to, examples, measures, problems, comparisons and history.

items.concept: Atlas Credits Prepaid Subscriptions and Overage
items.summary: Atlas bills against five subscription types: Elastic (a monthly invoice for usage, no commitment), Prepaid (credits bought up front for a chosen term), Flex Commitment (unused credits are charged in the last month of the term), Monthly Commitment (the greater of usage or the prorated monthly commitment, with unused credits covering later overages) and Marketplace. Available credits are drawn down in the order shown in the Available Credits table; when a Monthly Commitment organization runs out of credits it transitions to Elastic Billing and usage beyond the credits is billed, and when a subscription expires Atlas charges remaining usage to the payment method on file and reverts paid support plans to Basic. This pack draws on 4 source pages across 2 host labels and covers definitions, structure, mechanism, how-to, examples, measures, problems and history; the only independent figures (a 3-year default commit with a 15 to 30 percent annual ramp) come from a buyer-side advisory firm and are marked unverified.

items.concept: Atlas Flex Pricing and Flex-vs-Dedicated Break-Even
items.summary: Atlas Flex is a usage-banded Atlas cluster tier billed hourly on operations per second: an $8 base for 100 ops/sec and 5 GB of storage, rising in $7, $6, $5 and $4 steps to 500 ops/sec and capped at $30 per month, which replaced the retired M2/M5 shared tiers and Serverless instances. At list price Flex is cheaper than the cheapest Dedicated tier (M10, $0.08/hr, "starts at $56.94/month" on the pricing page and "$60" in the Flex costs doc) at every load it can serve, so the move to Dedicated is driven by limits (5 GB storage, a 500 ops/sec hard limit with per-connection cooldown) and unsupported features rather than cost. The pack draws on 6 sources (MongoDB docs, pricing page, a MongoDB blog post, a MongoDB support FAQ and one third-party blog) and covers definitions, parameters, mechanism, how-to, examples, measures, problems, comparisons and history, with 3 flagged disagreements.

items.concept: Atlas Search and Dedicated Search Nodes Cost
items.summary: Atlas Search adds no fee when mongot is co-located with mongod, but co-located search shares cluster CPU and RAM and is documented for testing and prototyping, while dedicated Search Nodes need an M10+ cluster, a minimum of two nodes (up to 32 per region per shard) and bill per node-hour by tier and node class (high-CPU, low-CPU, storage-optimized). List prices differ by cloud (high-CPU S20 is $0.12/hr on AWS us-east-1, $0.14 on Google Cloud, $0.15 on Azure), search-to-database transfer appears under cluster network charges, and per-region node counts and the S10 tier are the newest cost levers. Drawn from 6 source pages, all MongoDB-authored, across measures, parameters, comparisons and problems; the pages disagree on the minimum production search tier (S20 versus the S10 announcement).

items.concept: Atlas Support Plan Pricing
items.summary: Atlas support is an organization-level paid subscription on top of usage: Basic is free, and the paid plans are Developer (30-day free trial, 8-hour initial response goal), Pro (first response from 2 hours) and Enterprise (30 minutes on the plans page, 15 minutes to 2 hours in the docs), with Platinum (15 minutes) also listed on the plans page. Neither the docs nor the plans page publishes prices; the only public formula is a January 2024 MongoDB staff forum reply (Developer the greater of $49 or 20% of total monthly charges, Pro the greater of $799 or 20%), and plan changes take effect on the first day of the next month while reactivation bills retroactively for up to 90 days. This pack draws on 5 source pages across 3 host labels and covers definitions, mechanism, parameters, how-to, measures, problems and comparisons, with 2 recorded disagreements.

items.concept: Billing Alerts and Budget Controls
items.summary: Atlas billing alerts are notification-only: they are created on the Organization Alerts page (or the Project Alerts page for project-level conditions) by choosing Target = Billing, with conditions such as credit card about to expire, amount billed yesterday, current bill for a project or the organization, and daily, weekly or monthly gross-spend or billing change; thresholds are USD amounts or percentages, and the sources document no setting that stops or pauses spend at a billing threshold. The one built-in cost ceiling they describe is the Flex cluster tier, priced at $8 to $30 per month and capped at $30 per month. This pack draws on 5 source pages across 2 host labels and covers definitions, mechanism, parameters, how-to, examples, measures, problems and comparisons.

items.concept: Cloud Marketplace Billing for Atlas (AWS GCP Azure)
items.summary: Atlas supports paying for usage through the AWS, Google Cloud and Azure marketplaces with self-serve Pay-as-You-Go listings that need no upfront commitment: the customer subscribes in the cloud console, links the marketplace billing account to one Atlas organization on the Select an Organization to Link page, and once the sync completes the marketplace subscription is listed as the Atlas payment method and the invoice comes from the marketplace. All outstanding or failed Atlas invoices must be resolved before linking, and unlinking is done in the cloud console (AWS Cancel Subscription, Azure Cancel subscription, GCP Cancel Purchase) without deleting Atlas resources, so charges continue. This pack draws on 6 source pages across 3 host labels and covers definitions, mechanism, how-to, measures, problems, comparisons and open questions; the Atlas pages do not describe private offers, marketplace contracts, commitment drawdown, required cloud roles or Azure and GCP invoice frequency.

items.concept: Cloudflare AI-crawler monetization & verification stack
items.summary: The stack Cloudflare built to answer three separated questions about AI crawler traffic — who is this crawler provably (Web Bot Auth, an RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures profile, feeding the BotBase behavior taxonomy of Verified Bots), may it have this content (AI Crawl Control's WAF-rule enforcement plus managed robots.txt and the Content Signals Policy, which are declarations, not enforcement), and at what price (Pay Per Crawl's HTTP 402 protocol, Stripe-settled with Cloudflare as Merchant of Record). Drawn from one 2026-09-02 research reference (10 sections, 81 footnotes) covering the default-block policy timeline, enforcement/evasion evidence (the Cloudflare vs Perplexity dispute), structural criticism (gatekeeper concentration, standards capture), and competing standards (RSL, TDMRep, ai.txt, AIPREF, x402).

items.concept: Cluster Tier Families and Hourly Pricing (General vs Low-CPU vs NVMe)
items.summary: An Atlas cluster tier sets the RAM, vCPUs and storage of each data-bearing server and is billed per instance hour; the same M-size comes as a General tier, a Low-CPU tier that keeps RAM and storage but halves vCPUs at a lower hourly price, and an NVMe tier on locally attached ephemeral SSD with fixed storage (AWS and Azure only). Drawn from 7 source pages (MongoDB Atlas docs, the MongoDB on AWS pricing page, a Vantage blog) across definitions, parameters, measures, problems, comparisons and how-to; the only public hourly prices found are January 2022 AWS us-east-1 figures.

items.concept: Cost Governance Guardrails (Resource Policies and IaC Cost Controls)
items.summary: Atlas cost guardrails are preventive or detective, and none hard-stops billing: the preventive control is Atlas Resource Policies, organization-level Cedar forbid-only rules that are allow-by-default and not retroactive and that cap cluster tier and auto-scaling bounds, disk size, clusters per project, topology, shard count, cloud provider and region, managed through the UI, the Atlas Administration API, Terraform (mongodbatlas_resource_policy), Pulumi or CloudFormation, while the detective controls are project-level "Monthly pending invoice" billing alerts, Cost Explorer, resource tags, and pausing or terminating dev and test clusters. The pack draws on 6 sources (MongoDB docs, MongoDB blog, Atlas Architecture Center, Pulumi registry, Foojay, MongoDB feedback portal) and covers definitions, parameters, mechanism, how-to, examples, problems and facts. It flags 1 disagreement, about whether a monthly project billing alert exists.

The pack draws on 4 contributing sources (almost entirely MongoDB docs, plus one DoiT page) and covers definitions, linking prerequisites and limits (including the 250-organization cap), proration examples, unlinking, and how Charts billing ingestion and the Admin API handle linked invoices.

items.concept: Cross-Vendor Document Database Pricing Comparison (DocumentDB Cosmos DB DynamoDB)
items.summary: Atlas competitors bill on different units: Amazon DocumentDB charges per instance-hour plus storage (Standard per-I/O or I/O-Optimized), Azure Cosmos DB charges per provisioned or consumed Request Unit plus storage in every replicated region, and DynamoDB charges per request unit on-demand or provisioned, with on-demand prices cut 50% from 2024-11-01. The two public Atlas-versus-competitor comparisons are vendor-authored and conflict: Microsoft claims Azure DocumentDB is 39-70% cheaper than Atlas on AWS, while Vantage found Amazon DocumentDB 26.7% dearer than Atlas, partly because Atlas includes replica nodes in its tier price. The pack holds 115 source-anchored units from 6 sources (5 hosts) across 10 facets, mostly vendor pricing-page rates and worked examples.

items.concept: Data Lifecycle Cost Model (TTL vs Online Archive vs Data Federation)
items.summary: The cost choices for aging MongoDB Atlas data: a TTL index deletes expired documents (the data is gone), Online Archive moves infrequently accessed data to managed, read-only cloud object storage where it stays queryable through a federated endpoint, and Atlas Data Federation queries archived data or your own S3 bucket and bills data processed and data returned. Drawn from 6 sources (MongoDB manual and Atlas billing docs, a community forum thread, a third-party blog), covering definitions, mechanisms, how-to, parameters, billing measures, limits and comparisons.

items.concept: EU AI Act Article 53(1)(c) TDM Opt-Out
items.summary: EU AI Act Article 53(1)(c) is the GPAI-provider duty to maintain a copyright policy that identifies and honours text-and-data-mining (TDM) rights reservations made under DSM Directive Art. 4(3). Machine-readable means (Recital 18) is the operative standard for online content; robots.txt/RFC 9309 is the only protocol named in the GPAI Code of Practice's Copyright chapter (Measure 1.3), while W3C TDMRep, Cloudflare Content Signals and IETF aipref are credible but unrecognised candidates, and llms.txt/ai.txt are not opt-outs at all. Kneschke v LAION (OLG Hamburg) held a reservation must be machine-actionable, not just machine-readable; GEMA v OpenAI shows the TDM exception does not shelter memorisation/regurgitation. Sourced from 3 files (1 skill + 2 references) in the eu-ai-act-tdm-opt-out skill, covering the DSM/AI-Act legal framework, the Code of Practice, case law, and the protocol layer.

items.summary: An orphaned exo runner is a model-runner child whose parent worker was hard-killed; it keeps running and holds Metal memory and, for multi-node instances, RDMA queue pairs, so the next runner on that node cannot finish JACCL setup.

items.concept: FinOps Framework Applied to Atlas
items.summary: The FinOps Foundation Framework 2025 adds Scopes (a segment of technology-related spending to which FinOps concepts are applied) and runs an iterative Inform, Optimize, Operate lifecycle over them; MongoDB publishes no official mapping of Atlas to that lifecycle, so any mapping is inference. Atlas supplies the Inform-phase data through Cost Explorer (grouping by organization, project, cluster and service), resource tags on invoice line items, cross-organization billing, and FOCUS 1.3 reports from the Invoices page or the FOCUS Data API, while third-party tools such as DoiT ingest the same data; a known gap is that tags are resolved at export time, so deleted clusters appear untagged. The pack draws on 6 sources (FinOps Foundation, Atlas billing docs, MongoDB blog, DoiT, MongoDB feedback portal) and covers definitions, structure, mechanism, how-to, parameters, measures, problems, comparisons and history, with 1 flagged disagreement about a workaround.

items.concept: Glean Enterprise CLI
items.summary: The glean CLI (gleanwork/glean-cli) is the vendor-published, agent-friendly command-line client for Glean enterprise search, chat, agents, and knowledge management, wrapping the Client API in three tiers (raw glean api, typed namespace commands, and ergonomic search/chat). Hands-on verification against a live authenticated tenant (v0.17.1) confirmed the documented capability map but surfaced several undocumented gotchas: --dry-run only previews a request's body (not full request detail, unlike --preview), chat --save defaults to true, the CLI is single-tenant with no profile support, search has no recency-sort flag, and the credential-resolution fallback (env to keyring to config file) does not fully account for one observed case where auth succeeded despite all three sources appearing empty. items.concept: Heart
items.summary: The heart is a hollow muscular organ of somewhat conical form lying between the lungs in the middle mediastinum, enclosed in the pericardium; it is the central organ of the blood vascular system, pumping blood through the arteries by its contraction, and is divided by septa into right and left halves, each with an atrium and a ventricle. One source (Gray's Anatomy 1918, Angiology) covers its definition, structure (chambers, valves, wall and conduction tissue, coronary vessels, pericardium), mechanism (development, cardiac cycle, fetal circulation), size and cycle timings, and the two malformations the text names.

items.concept: Indexing
items.summary: An index is a data structure the database keeps sorted so it can find and order documents or rows without scanning the whole collection or table, at the cost of extra writes and storage. Compiled from 9 sources (MongoDB manual and docs, Prisma, Drizzle, Nile/Postgres, Turso/SQLite, Convex, InstantDB, MotherDuck): index types (B-tree, hash, GIN/GiST/SP-GiST/BRIN/bloom, compound, unique, partial, multikey, wildcard, text, geospatial, TTL, hidden, HNSW/IVFFlat), how the query planner chooses and uses an index (explain plans, IXSCAN vs COLLSCAN, covered queries, selectivity, the ESR guideline, hints), how ORMs declare indexes (@@index, index()/uniqueIndex(), .index()/withIndex), and the failure modes (unused or redundant indexes, write overhead, in-memory sorts, full scans).

items.concept: llms.txt
items.summary: llms.txt is a proposed markdown-based discovery file - an H1 title, an optional blockquote summary, and H2-organized markdown link lists - placed at a site's root or subpath so language models and AI agents can get a curated, priority-ordered map of a site's content instead of crawling raw HTML; llms-full.txt (an unofficial companion inlining the whole docset) and split variants (llms-small.txt, per-page .md twins) round out the family. Now at spec v2 (llmstxt.org, modified 2026-08-10), it remains an unratified community proposal with real but modest adoption (roughly 5-10% of the general web, higher among SEO-savvy/docs-platform sites), no official validator, and mixed evidence that major AI crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot) actually fetch or prioritize it over robots.txt/sitemap.xml - Google and others have publicly said they do not consume it specially. Generation is largely automatic on docs platforms (Mintlify, GitBook, Fern, ReadMe) and via static-site-generator plugins or crawl-based tools (Firecrawl, llms_txt2ctx), with recreation for third-party sites treated as a low-risk link-list-plus-descriptions exercise. Summarized from 5 sources (4 hub reference files plus the llms-explorer repo's own spec.md writeup), covering structure, mechanism, measures, problems, comparisons and facts facets.

items.concept: Matryoshka Dimension Truncation for Vector Storage Cost
items.summary: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) trains an embedding model so that a leading prefix of the vector is itself a usable shorter embedding; truncating to 256, 512 or 1024 dimensions and re-normalizing cuts vector storage and index RAM roughly linearly at a small retrieval-quality cost, and stacks with Atlas automatic scalar (about 1/3.75 RAM) and binary (1/24 RAM) quantization. The pack draws on 5 sources (Voyage AI and Atlas Vector Search docs, an OpenAI post, a May 2026 arXiv study via a summary site, and a ZeroEntropy vendor post) and records one disagreement over whether truncation needs Matryoshka-trained models.

items.concept: MongoDB Compound Index Design: ESR, Selectivity, Covering and Multikey Bounds
items.summary: A compound index stores references ordered by several fields; key order (equality fields first, then sort, then range — the ESR guideline), selectivity, prefix rules, covered queries, multikey index bounds with $elemMatch and partial/sparse filter semantics decide whether a query can use the index and how many keys and documents it examines. Compiled from MongoDB manual and Atlas pages plus the run's verified claims.

Compiled from MongoDB manual, Atlas and Compass pages plus the run's verified claims; facets cover definitions, mechanisms, how-tos, problems and version changes.

items.concept: MongoDB Query Shape Optimization: Sort, Pagination, Operators and Sharded Targeting
items.summary: The shape of a find or aggregate query decides whether the planner can use an index: index-backed sorts avoid the blocking SORT stage and its memory limit, keyset pagination replaces deep skip, $regex, $ne, $nin, $where and $expr constrain index bounds, $in and $or become point bounds or index unions, projection can make a query covered, count, distinct, $sample and cursor batchSize/maxTimeMS carry their own costs, and a sharded query is targeted only when the shard key is in the filter. Compiled from MongoDB manual and Atlas pages plus the run's verified claims.

items.concept: MongoDB Wildcard and Hidden Indexes, Index Builds and Index Overhead
items.summary: Wildcard indexes index every scalar value under a path so queries on unknown field names can use an index, hidden indexes stay fully maintained but invisible to the planner, and index builds run as optimized hybrid builds that replica-set members vote to commit under a commit quorum; every index adds disk, cache and write cost. Compiled from MongoDB manual and Atlas pages plus the run's verified claims.

items.concept: Multi-Region and Cross-Cloud Data Transfer Costs
items.summary: Atlas passes cloud-provider data transfer charges through to customers, tabulated daily by provider and by the regions of the source and destination nodes, and the MongoDB on AWS pricing page lists $0.01/GB same region, $0.02/GB cross-region and $0.09/GB internet. For most customers transfer is under 10% of the bill, multi-region clusters can cost more depending on the added regions, queries from on-premises, across cloud providers or between continents cost the most, and replication and heartbeat traffic is billed on the Same Region line. Drawn from 5 source pages (Atlas docs, the MongoDB on AWS pricing page, a 2020 forum thread, an AWS NLB billing notice, a 2019 blog) across measures, mechanism, how-to, problems and comparisons; two disagreements are listed.

items.concept: NLWeb and MCP as agentic-discovery alternatives to llms.txt
items.summary: NLWeb is R.V. Guha's schema.org/RSS query layer, launched by Microsoft in 2025-05 and transferred to the independent nlweb-ai org in 2025-07-30; every instance also exposes a version-pinned (2024-11-05), stateless, undiscoverable MCP /mcp route whose auth fails open, and the repo's main branch has been feature-dormant since 2026-06-10. Sourced from one reference document (14 footnoted sources, 90 scanned units, 74 kept) that frames NLWeb, MCP, and WebMCP not as competitors to a static llms.txt but as complementary layers, and closes with a default-plus-triggers decision rule: publish llms.txt always, and add a live endpoint only against six named triggers a file structurally cannot satisfy (auth/entitlements, actions, an unenumerable corpus, minute-scale volatility, metering, or wanting query-intent signal).

items.concept: Ollama core platform
items.summary: Ollama is a local LLM runtime whose core platform is a native REST API (/api/generate, /api/chat with NDJSON streaming, errors and usage fields), a Modelfile build format (FROM, PARAMETER, TEMPLATE, SYSTEM, ADAPTER), a Docker-v2-style registry with content-addressed blobs and manifests, GGUF/safetensors import and quantization tags, LoRA adapters, OpenAI and Anthropic compatible endpoints, and a think capability. Compiled from 44 source files (cached /dr page bodies, /dr claim units and the docs.ollama.com mirror) across 20 hosts.

items.concept: Ollama deployment and operations
items.summary: Ollama deployment and operations covers running Ollama in Docker and Kubernetes (otwld Helm chart, GPU passthrough, model volumes, OLLAMA_HOST binding), the embeddings API and local RAG, local embeddings into MongoDB Atlas Vector Search, Ollama cloud models and the cloud API (ollama signin, OLLAMA_API_KEY, usage limits), the web_search and web_fetch API, security hardening and CVEs (CVE-2026-7482 fixed in 0.17.1), observability (logs, /api/ps, Prometheus exporters, OpenTelemetry) and air-gapped model mirroring (offline directory copy, private-registry and pull-through limits), drawn from the official docs.ollama.com pages plus community guides, advisories and a research claim set.

items.concept: Ollama deployment, cloud, security and operations
items.summary: Ollama deployment and operations covers running Ollama in Docker and Kubernetes (otwld Helm chart, GPU passthrough, model volumes, OLLAMA_HOST binding), the embeddings API and local RAG, local embeddings into MongoDB Atlas Vector Search, Ollama cloud models and the cloud API (ollama signin, OLLAMA_API_KEY, usage limits), the web_search and web_fetch API, security hardening and CVEs (CVE-2026-7482 fixed in 0.17.1), observability (logs, /api/ps, Prometheus exporters, OpenTelemetry) and air-gapped model mirroring (offline directory copy, private-registry and pull-through limits), drawn from the official docs.ollama.com pages plus community guides, advisories and a research claim set.

items.concept: Ollama engine architecture
items.summary: Ollama's inference engine has changed over time: a May 2025 blog introduced Ollama's own new engine built on the GGML tensor library for multimodal models. Commit 9db4bdb (PR #16031, merged 2026-05-29, first in v0.30.0-rc32 and v0.30.0) removed the native Go engine and the vendored llama.cpp backend: GGUF models now run on upstream llama-server, pinned by LLAMA_CPP_VERSION, with a temporary compatibility layer, and safetensors models run on the MLX engine on Apple Silicon (the default there since v0.40.0). The runner is chosen per manifest (mlx, llamacpp or ggml) by runnerPreferences(). Units describing the native engine are marked as history.

items.summary: GGUF (GPT-Unified Format) is the binary format used by llama.cpp and Ollama to store quantized model weights for efficient CPU and GPU inference. The conversion script takes the merged 16-bit PyTorch model produced by training and converts it to a self-contained GGUF file at a target quantization level. (from stratospherelinuxips.readthedocs.io)

items.concept: Ollama integrations and ecosystem
items.summary: Ollama integrations are the tools and libraries that connect to a local or cloud Ollama server. The ollama launch command sets up and runs coding tools such as Claude Code, OpenCode and Codex with local or cloud models; the Go api package, ollama-python and ollama-js read OLLAMA_HOST; langchain-ollama provides ChatOllama; editors (Cline, Roo Code, Zed, JetBrains, VS Code), MCP bridges (ollmcp, MCPHost), agent harnesses (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi) and n8n nodes connect through the native or OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Sources: docs.ollama.com plus vendor docs, READMEs and community posts.

items.concept: RamaLama and the Ollama registry
items.summary: RamaLama is an open-source tool that runs and serves AI models in OCI containers (Podman or Docker), pulling them from transports selected by prefix (ollama://, huggingface://, oci://, modelscope://, rlcr://, URLs). Through v0.20.0 an unprefixed model name used the Ollama transport; v0.21.0 (2026-05-14) began deprecating it, v0.23.0 (2026-06-24) relaxed that, and the code at v0.25.0 has no implicit default (names with a slash go to Hugging Face, unknown shortnames raise an error), although the README still says org-less names default to Ollama. Containers are rootless and locked down by default. Sources span GitHub (README, releases, pull requests, source), man pages, Red Hat, a blog and a forum thread.

items.concept: Ollama templates and scale-out
items.summary: The Modelfile TEMPLATE instruction holds the full, model-specific prompt template that Ollama sends to the model, written in Go template syntax with system, prompt, response, messages, tools and suffix variables; `ollama show --template` prints a model's shipped template. Scale-out covers Ollama's per-server concurrency settings (OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL, OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS, OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE), vLLM data-parallel load-balancing modes, LiteLLM router strategies and two independent Ollama-versus-vLLM benchmarks, across 8 hosts.

items.concept: Ollama web search and web fetch API

Two of the three docsets contributed (the OpenAI export is empty).

items.concept: Query Efficiency as a Cost Lever
items.summary: Inefficient queries (collection scans, high scanned-to-returned ratios) burn CPU, disk I/O and WiredTiger cache, which can push a team toward a larger Atlas cluster tier; Atlas surfaces the signal through Query Targeting alerts (default 1000:1, ideal near 1), the Query Profiler and Performance Advisor index suggestions ranked by Impact, covered queries skip document reads, and every unused or redundant index adds write cost, storage and cache pressure. Drawn from 7 sources (MongoDB Atlas and manual pages, a community forum thread, Netdata and OneUptime guides, a third-party blog), covering definitions, mechanisms, parameters, how-to, measures and problems; no source states a measured tier reduction from tuning, and the evidence on the write penalty of many indexes is thin and disputed.

items.concept: Really Simple Licensing (RSL)
items.summary: Really Simple Licensing (RSL) is an open XML standard (launched 2025-09-10, RSL 1.0 Recommendation 2025-12-10, governed by the RSL Technical Steering Committee and the RSL Collective) for expressing machine-readable licensing, payment, and legal terms for digital content, discovered chiefly through a new robots.txt License: directive and composing with — not replacing — robots.txt, llms.txt, ai.txt, IETF AIPREF, Cloudflare Content Signals, W3C TDMRep, and C2PA/CAWG. Drawn from 4 sources covering the specification itself, deployment/tooling/anti-patterns, the standards landscape, and measured adoption/legal weight, this pack shows RSL as a well-engineered declaration layer with thin real-world uptake: direct measurement found roughly 3 independent publisher deployments (of which most are non-conformant with the spec's own rules), no AI company has agreed to honor it, and its legal force stands on notice/evidentiary value and an EU DSM Art. 4(3) reservation rather than technical enforcement.

items.concept: Region and Cloud Provider Price Differentials for Atlas
items.summary: Atlas prices differ by cloud provider (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) and by region: the Atlas docs state that the provider and region choice affects the cost of a cluster, and the pricing page quotes dedicated-tier base prices for one reference region per provider (AWS us-east-1, Azure eastus2, Google Cloud us-central1) while only Online Archive lists rates region by region. Backup storage, data transfer (cheapest within a region, dearest across providers or to the Internet) and multi-region nodes also vary by provider and region. The pack holds 85 source-anchored units from 5 sources (4 hosts) across 9 facets, mostly measures and facts.

items.concept: Replica Set Node Topology Cost
items.summary: An Atlas replica set's cost scales with the number and tier of its data-bearing nodes: electable nodes must total 3, 5 or 7, read-only and analytics nodes add capacity without voting, and each data-bearing node is billed at the cluster tier's hourly rate plus its storage. Analytics nodes can use a different tier priced prorated per node, while arbiters are documented only for self-managed sets and the sources disagree on whether the three-node minimum is justified for test environments. Drawn from 9 source pages (MongoDB Atlas docs, manual and blog, forum threads, IBM Community and oneuptime blogs) across definitions, parameters, mechanism, problems and how-to.

items.concept: Resource Tags and Cost Allocation (Showback/Chargeback)
items.summary: Atlas resource tags are case-sensitive key-value pairs added to projects and clusters; Atlas copies cluster tags onto billing output (a Tag/<key> column in the invoice CSV and a tags field on Admin API invoice line items) so teams can build showback or chargeback reports, but tags are read when the CSV is generated or the API is called, so retagging mid-cycle rewrites the invoice view and clusters deleted before the export appear untagged. The FinOps Framework frames the same practice as allocation (apportioning costs to those responsible for them), built on an allocation strategy, a tagging strategy and a shared-cost strategy. This pack draws on 7 source pages across 4 host labels and covers definitions, structure, mechanism, parameters, how-to, examples, measures, problems, comparisons and history.

items.concept: robots.txt and the Content-Signal AI-preference extension
items.summary: robots.txt is the Robots Exclusion Protocol (RFC 9309, Sept 2022, Proposed Standard): a crawl-access file of User-agent groups with Allow/Disallow rules, MUST-level wildcards (*, $), octet-based longest-match precedence with an allow-wins SHOULD tie-break, a 500 KiB parsing floor, and explicit non-goals (it is not access authorization). Riding inside it is a newer, unstandardized AI-preference layer — Cloudflare's Content-Signal (search/ai-input/ai-train, plus a testing content-use field) and its IETF successor draft (Content-Usage, AIPREF) — which states what a crawler may do with content after fetching it, has no announced enforcing consumer, and is evidenced (Perplexity dispute, Consent in Crisis study, Google's 'no effects whatsoever') to be a stated preference rather than a technical control. Drawn from two /dr-authored references (RFC 9309 spec analysis and the Content-Signal/AIPREF layer), 34 sourced footnotes.

items.concept: router top-k agreement under quantization as a diagnostic
items.summary: Why top-k is a cliff: the router picks experts with a hard top-k on scores, so a small perturbation of hidden state or router logits flips an expert only when it moves the k-th and (k+1)-th scores across each other. The change in computation is then a different expert, not a small numeric error. ...

items.concept: Scheduled and Predictive Scaling for Atlas Cost
items.summary: Atlas has no documented native time-of-day tier schedule, so time-pattern cost control comes from two mechanisms: predictive auto-scaling, which scales eligible clusters up ahead of forecast cyclical spikes and never scales down, and customer-run pause and resume schedules for non-production dedicated clusters, where a paused cluster is charged for storage only and auto-resumes after 30 days. Reactive scale-down stays conservative (a 24-hour cooldown and 4-hour low-load window), so spiky batch workloads can sit on a larger tier for many hours. The pack holds 127 source-anchored units from 8 sources (5 hosts: MongoDB docs and engineering blog, a prototype write-up, a third-party pause guide, a customer feedback thread) across 11 facets, with 2 conflicts over scale-down rules and prototype versus shipped planner behavior.

items.concept: Schema Design for Storage Cost
items.summary: Schema design changes MongoDB storage bytes because BSON is self-describing: every document stores its own field names, so field-name length, value types (int32 versus string IDs, Date versus string), explicit nulls, stray metadata fields such as spring-data _class, and unneeded indexes all add on-disk size, while WiredTiger block compression shrinks the field-name effect sharply and bloated documents mainly cost RAM rather than disk. Drawn from 6 sources (Allegro and Percona measurements, MongoDB manual anti-pattern pages and a MongoDB 3.0 compression blog), covering definitions, mechanisms, measures, problems and comparisons; the sources disagree on how much short field names still save under compression.

items.concept: Self-Managed MongoDB vs Atlas TCO
items.summary: Comparing self-managed MongoDB with Atlas on sticker price favors self-hosting (an illustrative 3-node Atlas M30 at about $1,180/month against about $440/month of self-hosted compute), but total cost of ownership also turns on ops labor, backup and PITR tooling, data transfer, Atlas-only features and Community Edition gaps such as no hot backup, PITR or official support. The sources disagree on which is cheaper: the Prosopo migration reports a 90% cut ($3,000+ to $160 per month on a single standalone server), OneUptime says self-hosting with labor often matches or exceeds Atlas for small teams, and MongoDB staff call Atlas the most cost-effective option for limited DBA and ops staff. The pack draws on 4 sources (one migration case study, two blogs including a competing vendor, and a 2021 forum thread) and covers definitions, structure, how-to, measures, problems and comparisons, with 3 flagged disagreements.

items.concept: Sharded Cluster Cost Economics
items.summary: Atlas bills a sharded cluster as replication factor times shard count data-bearing nodes at the chosen tier, plus three config servers at a separate rate that tier and storage choices do not change; the billing page does not mention a mongos charge. Every shard must have the same node counts, storage and NVMe tier, though shards can run different compute tiers under independent shard scaling, and MongoDB advises adding a shard at sustained 60-70% utilization while MongoDB 8.0 config shards remove the dedicated config server cost for small clusters. Drawn from 6 source pages (MongoDB Atlas docs and manual, Jira) across definitions, structure, parameters, measures, problems and comparisons; the manual's advice to start sharded and Jira's report that a one-shard M30 costs twice a replica set are listed as a disagreement.

items.concept: Storage Growth and IOPS Forecasting for Cost
items.summary: On Atlas Core dedicated clusters, storage is billed on the full provisioned amount, and storage auto-scaling is on by default, triggers at 90% used on any node, sizes the new disk to 70% used and only scales up, which can force a tier upgrade when the disk would exceed the tier's maximum. IOPS is tied to disk size on Gen1, Azure and GCP, while Gen2 Dedicated clusters bill a size-based baseline plus separately billed IOPS; storage cannot be shrunk in place, so Atlas provisions new volumes and resyncs with per-node downtime, and AWS EBS limits volume modifications to four per rolling 24 hours. Drawn from 6 source pages (Atlas docs, the AWS EBS guide, a MongoDB forum thread) across measures, problems, parameters and mechanism; the sources disagree on whether storage can be reduced in place.

items.concept: Tensor-parallel all-reduce count per transformer layer in MLX shard_linear

items.concept: Terraform Tag Enforcement and Policy-as-Code for Atlas Cost
items.summary: Atlas resource tags are key-value pairs on clusters that flow into invoice CSVs and the Admin API pending-invoice lineItems.tags field, so MongoDB recommends enforcing mandatory tags and managing them through Terraform; the mongodbatlas provider exposes tags as a set of objects and has no AWS-style default_tags, leaving enforcement to modules plus plan-time Sentinel or OPA policy in HCP Terraform, for which no Atlas-specific example was found. The pack draws on 6 source URLs (Atlas tags docs, the invoice-tags GA post, the Architecture Center, provider issue 2006, HCP Terraform policy docs and the AWS default_tags post) across definitions, tag rules and limits, billing behaviour, provider limitations and policy mechanics.

items.concept: Thunderbolt eGPU on Linux for local LLM inference
items.summary: What it takes to run an NVIDIA GPU in a Thunderbolt/USB4 enclosure on Linux and have Ollama use it, distilled from a September 2026 RTX 5080 / Razer Core X V2 / ASUS NUC 15 Pro (Arrow Lake, Thunderbolt 4, Ubuntu 26.04, kernel 7.0, driver 610-open) debugging session and the kernel, NVIDIA, ASUS and community sources it leaned on. Covers how the PCIe tunnel is built and why the Linux thunderbolt driver's host_reset rebuilds it, the kernel parameters that keep the BIOS tunnel (host_reset=0, realloc=off, clx=0), hotplug BAR sizing versus decode failures, a driverless MMIO chip-ID probe with per-hop Unsupported-Request localisation, NVIDIA driver blocking and power-management options for an eGPU, a systemd loader ordered after bolt, how to prove Ollama is on CUDA, and the ASUS iSetupCfg BIOS CLI. For anyone whose eGPU enumerates but reads 0xffffffff; verified-as-of 2026-09-24.

items.concept: Vector Search Quantization and Embedding Storage Cost
items.summary: Atlas Vector Search can shrink embedding memory with automatic scalar (int8) or binary (int1) quantization or by ingesting pre-quantized BSON binData vectors, cutting mongot RAM by 3.75x for scalar and 24x for binary because the HNSW graph itself does not shrink. Full-fidelity vectors stay on disk for rescoring and exact search, so disk use does not fall and the Atlas UI Size metric can rise, while the Required Memory metric estimates query-time RAM. Binary quantization needs rescoring and suits high-dimension, zero-centred embeddings, and all savings figures are vendor-reported; this pack draws on 4 source pages (MongoDB docs and blog, Elastic, Azure AI Search) across mechanism, measures, comparisons, parameters and history.

items.concept: WiredTiger Block and Prefix Compression as Storage Cost Lever
items.summary: WiredTiger compresses MongoDB collection data with block compression (snappy by default, zlib and zstd optional, zstd by default for time series collections) and compresses index keys with prefix compression (on by default), which cuts on-disk bytes and so the provisioned storage bill at the price of extra CPU; collection data stays uncompressed in the WiredTiger cache. Drawn from 6 sources (MongoDB manual and FAQ, WiredTiger documentation, a Percona benchmark, two third-party blogs), covering definitions, mechanisms, parameters, how-to, measures, problems and comparisons; the sources disagree on whether compact recompresses existing data and on typical compression ratios.
